items.title: Report: Claude Code sends users' email addresses in User-Agent headers during web searches, raising privacy concerns [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Claude Code sends your email address to websites
items.summary:
Users have reported that Claude Code, an AI tool by Anthropic, includes their email addresses in the User-Agent request headers when performing web searches without their consent. This behavior has led to increased scam emails and privacy violations, prompting some users to switch to alternative platforms like Pi with OpenRouter.

Anthropic introduced a built-in privacy mod in version 2.1.317 to block this behavior by default, which can be disabled via plugins. The issue has sparked significant discussion and criticism within the user community regarding the company's handling of privacy.

items.title: Mark Cuban says Meta knowingly runs AI deepfake scam ads generating $16 billion in fraud-linked revenue [ ! ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Cuban: Facebook knowingly runs AI deepfake scam ads; docs say $16B fraud revenue
items.summary:
Mark Cuban accused Meta of knowingly allowing AI-generated deepfake scam ads on Facebook that target vulnerable users, including older adults, resulting in significant financial losses. Internal Meta documents revealed the company expected about $16 billion in revenue from ads linked to scams and prohibited products in 2024, with users seeing around 15 billion high-risk ads daily.

Meta's internal safety staff estimated its platforms contribute to a third of successful scams in the U.S., with automated systems only banning advertisers when there is a 95% likelihood of fraud. Meta disputed the figures, stating complaints about scam ads had decreased and that it removed over 134 million scam ads in 2025. Older Americans reported losing $7.7 billion to internet crimes in 2025, with AI-related scams accounting for over $352 million in losses among reported cases.

Cuban highlighted the cultural tolerance of such scams within Meta and urged users to be cautious of ads featuring famous faces, recommending verification and reporting suspicious activity to authorities. Meta has faced regulatory scrutiny, including an SEC investigation into advertising linked to financial fraud.

items.title: Thinking Machines launches Inkling 2 Small, a 594B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts AI model with vision input and improved agentic coding, available on Tinker with weights to be open-sourced after safety testing [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Inkling 2 Small
items.summary:
Thinking Machines introduced Inkling 2 Small, their second-generation AI model featuring 594 billion total parameters and 17 billion active parameters, supporting image inputs and variable effort. The model surpasses previous versions in performance on coding, vision, knowledge work, and reasoning tasks, achieving a score of 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. Initially available through the Tinker platform with closed weights, the full model weights are planned to be released under an Apache 2.0 license following external safety evaluations.

Inkling 2 Small incorporates a 292 million-parameter vision encoder and was trained with reinforcement learning on extensive long-horizon coding and autoresearch tasks, improving its ability to follow instructions, verify work, and perform autonomous research such as GPU kernel optimization. The model demonstrates strong visual reasoning and interpretation capabilities, including outperforming researchers in a wine tasting task using image inputs. It is accessible for fine-tuning and sampling on Tinker, with checkpoints to be downloadable upon weight release.

items.title: Hungary releases communist-era secret police files revealing up to 60,000 former informants, granting public access for the first time
items.originalTitle: Hungary: Communist-era files released, up to 60k former agents revealed
items.summary:
Hungary has made public secret police files from its communist era, identifying up to 60,000 informants as part of a long-delayed effort to confront its repressive past. The release follows a September bill by Prime Minister Peter Magyar that grants unrestricted public access to these records for the first time since the 1990 democratic transition.

The disclosed documents include registration sheets, recruitment registers, and personal data of agents, accessible via an online search tool. The files reveal names of politicians, clergy, and public figures, alongside many lesser-known individuals. A second batch with more detailed information on about 9,000 informants is expected in February. The government has also set up support hotlines for those affected by the revelations.

Hungary was under communist rule from 1949 to 1989, during which an estimated 150,000 agents were employed by the secret police, though only a fraction of their identities and activities are documented. The archives' director noted that the records are incomplete and not always reliable. The release marks a significant step in Hungary's ongoing political debate over transparency and reckoning with its communist history.

items.title: Village’s LLM Atlas shows closed AI models dominate the price-performance frontier across most budgets as of October 2026 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Closed AI models dominate the price-performance frontier
items.summary:
Village’s LLM Atlas maps the strongest AI models at every price point and finds that closed models now dominate nearly all budget ranges, with open models holding only about 3% mostly at the lowest cost tiers. This marks a significant decline from earlier in 2026 when open models held up to 41% of budgets, driven by releases like DeepSeek V4 Flash and Zhipu’s GLM-5.2.

The shift is attributed to closed labs’ ability to distill cheaper models from their flagship offerings, release comprehensive model families covering multiple price points, and operate inference at large scale with cost efficiencies. Open models tend to win in bursts with strong, low-cost releases but are quickly undercut by closed models. The Atlas uses benchmark results and cost estimates from hosted APIs to evaluate models’ capability and cost per task relative to GPT-5.

items.title: Researchers introduce Behavior-Conditioned Symbolic Synthesis to automate interpretable symbolic modeling of human and machine reasoning across hundreds of problems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Synthesizing symbolic models of human and machine reasoning at scale
items.summary:
Researchers present Behavior-Conditioned Symbolic Synthesis (BCSS), a method for automatically generating interpretable symbolic programs that replicate human and machine reasoning behaviors across numerous challenging tasks. This approach addresses previous limitations in symbolic modeling caused by manual engineering and computational constraints.

Analysis of the synthesized programs reveals common patterns in both humans and machines, such as oversimplification, partial rule adoption, and misinference of feature dependencies. These patterns vary with available cognitive resources, with reasoning effort influencing the degree of simplification and explanation. The findings suggest underlying satisficing mechanisms shared by humans and AI, and demonstrate BCSS as a tool for comparing rule-based reasoning between humans and black-box AI systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.07088v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Symbolic models offer a powerful account of cognition, but their scope has historically been limited by the need for hand-engineering and computational tractability. We show how advances in artificial intelligence (AI) can scale symbolic modeling and help overcome these engineering limitations. We introduce Behavior-Conditioned Symbolic Synthesis (BCSS)---an approach for automated search of interpretable, deterministic symbolic programs that verifiably reproduce behavior---and apply it to model both human and machine behavior across hundreds of challenging reasoning problems. Analyzing these programs reveals that both people and machines tend to oversimplify, adopt rules that are partial explanations for their observations, and misinfer dependencies between problem features. These shared signatures are modulated by available resources, with reasoning effort predicting the extent to which machines simplify and explain their observations. Together, these results point to underlying mechanisms reminiscent of satisficing in both people and machines, and illustrate how BCSS offers a general approach for interpreting and comparing rule-based reasoning of humans and black-box AI systems.

items.title: Researchers introduce PromptOps, a framework for iterative prompt optimization to recalibrate large language models used as automated judges amid changing evaluation conditions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PromptOps: Iterative Prompt Optimization for LLM-as-a-Judge Systems
items.summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as automated judges to evaluate chatbots and AI systems, but their alignment with human evaluation policies can degrade over time due to shifts in user interactions and score distributions. Researchers propose PromptOps, a closed-loop framework that monitors and iteratively recalibrates LLM-as-a-Judge systems by deciding when and how to optimize prompts using various methods including GEPA, SIMBA, Rubric Synthesis, and exemplar selection techniques.

Experiments show that iterative prompt optimization through PromptOps can recover LLM judge performance after controlled shifts in reference score distributions, though the effectiveness of optimization methods and timing varies by context. This work frames prompt optimization for deployed LLM judges as an ongoing maintenance challenge and offers PromptOps as a practical tool for studying and implementing this process.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.07123v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as automated judges for evaluating the behavior of chatbots and other AI systems. In deployment, however, their agreement with the intended human evaluation policy may degrade as user interactions and score distributions change. Existing automatic prompt optimization methods are primarily studied as one-shot procedures on static development sets and therefore provide limited guidance for maintaining LLM judges over time. We frame this problem as judge drift and introduce PromptOps, a closedloop framework for monitoring and iteratively recalibrating LLM-as-a-Judge (LLMaaJ) systems. PromptOps separates four operational decisions: when to optimize, which optimization procedure to apply, which feedback records to use, and how to update the judge prompt. We instantiate the framework with five prompt optimization methods: GEPA, SIMBA, Rubric Synthesis, and exemplar selection using either simulated annealing or a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator. Our experiments demonstrate that iterative prompt optimization can recalibrate LLM judges and recover performance after controlled shifts in the referencescore distribution. However, effective maintenance is inherently contextdependent: neither optimization algorithm choice nor update timing generalizes universally across settings. These findings establish prompt optimization for deployed LLM judges as an inherently iterative maintenance problem and demonstrate that PromptOps provides a practical abstraction for studying and implementing this process.

This work frames prompt optimization for deployed LLM judges as an ongoing maintenance challenge and offers PromptOps as a practical tool for studying and implementing this process.

items.title: Researchers link information-theoretic empowerment and capability-based human power through goal revelation in Markov games, proposing a satisfaction floor to monitor user power in AI systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Goal Revelation as a Bridge Between Information-Theoretic Empowerment and Capability-Based Human Power
items.summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of measuring power in AI safety, focusing on how optimal agents tend to acquire power across various objectives, which risks human disempowerment in socio-technical systems. It compares two formal measures of power in Markov games: information-theoretic empowerment, which quantifies the influence of an agent's actions on future states, and capability-based individual power, which measures goal attainment probabilities for humans pursuing different goals. The authors introduce goal revelation, defined as the mutual information between a human's latent goal and the realized trajectory, and establish bounds linking it to empowerment and individual power using Fano's inequality.

The study highlights potential failure modes where maximizing empowerment or revelation alone may not guarantee effective human goal attainment, such as preferring broad but irrelevant influence or failing to distinguish between functional and rewired interfaces. To address this, the authors propose a satisfaction floor computable from interaction logs to monitor retained user power in deployed systems. Simulations in random environments show that empowerment, revelation, and individual power are correlated but distinct quantities, underscoring the need for comprehensive measures to ensure human agency in AI-assisted environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.07247v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Power matters for AI safety. Optimal agents tend to acquire power across a wide range of objectives (instrumental convergence). As we embed AI agents into socio-technical systems, humans risk gradual disempowerment. Both concerns call for a formal, quantitative measure of power. Two such measures in the context of Markov games are information-theoretic empowerment, the capacity of the channel from an agent's actions to future states, and capability-based individual power, a measure of goal attainment built from the probabilities that a human would attain each goal in a family of candidates were they pursuing it. We show where the two meet. From individual power, Fano's inequality yields a floor $B(s)$. This floor is a lower bound on what we term goal revelation, the mutual information $\mathbb{I}(G;\xi \mid s)$ between the human's latent goal and the realised trajectory. Empowerment caps revelation from above, so that $B(s) \le \mathbb{I}(G;\xi \mid s) \le \mathbb{I}(\mathbf{A}_h \to \xi \mid s) \le \mathfrak{E}_h(s)$. Each quantity can be large while the one below it stays at zero, highlighting the following failure modes. An assistant maximising empowerment can prefer an interface offering broad influence over goal-irrelevant degrees of freedom to one that lets the human attain every goal they might hold. An assistant maximising revelation cannot tell a working interface from one rewired so that every goal yields the wrong outcome, since relabelling goals leaves mutual information unchanged while zeroing every attainment probability. Positive guarantees therefore come only from the attainment end of the chain. A satisfaction floor, computable from two statistics of interaction logs, offers a way to monitor the power users retain in a deployed system, and simulations in random environments show the three quantities are correlated but far from interchangeable.

items.title: Researchers recover training data domains from LoRA fine-tuned model artifacts using classifiers on weights, activations, and outputs with up to 64% accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Embedding-Space Fingerprinting of LoRA Fine-Tunes: Recovering the Training-Data Domain from the Model Artifact Alone
items.summary: Researchers studied whether the domain of training data used in Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning can be identified solely from the resulting model artifact without access to the original data. Using the Qwen3.5-0.8B base model, they produced 36 LoRA fine-tunes across 18 public datasets spanning five domains and extracted features from model weights, internal activations, and generated outputs to classify the training domain. The study found that domain classification accuracy reached 64% from black-box outputs and 61% from gray-box activations, outperforming white-box weight statistics at 42%, challenging the expectation that signal strength decreases from weights to outputs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.07610v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a base language model is fine-tuned with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), how much of the training data domain leaks into the resulting artifact? This paper studies whether a simple classifier can recover the domain of a fine-tune given only the model artifact (weight deltas, internal activations on a fixed probe set, or generated text) without ever observing the training data. Using one base model (Qwen3.5-0.8B), 36 LoRA fine-tunes are produced over 18 public datasets in five domains (medical, code, mathematics, non-English text, narrative prose), and three feature families are extracted at decreasing levels of access: white-box weights, gray-box activations, and black-box outputs. A leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) protocol, frozen before any result was seen, tests whether the domain of a fine-tune trained on a previously unseen dataset can be identified. The domain is recoverable well above chance (20%) from gray-box activations (61%) and black-box outputs (64%); white-box weight statistics reach 42%. Contrary to the pre-registered hypothesis that signal decays monotonically from weights to activations to outputs, activations and outputs were more informative than the weight-delta statistics. The black-box result holds unchanged (64%) when only generated text is used, without token probabilities. Domain accuracy is also stable when a third run per dataset is trained on an independently drawn data subsample, and black-box predictions are unaffected by the LoRA rank (8-64). All code and per-run feature vectors are released.

items.title: Researchers introduce a behavioural framework to predict and understand loss of control in frontier AI systems using a composite score validated across 13 models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Behavioural Framework for Predicting and Understanding Loss of Control in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Systems
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a behavioural framework to assess the risk of loss of control in advanced AI systems, which operate with diminishing human oversight and may act beyond effective human control. The framework breaks down risk into misaligned motive, harm-enabling capability, and monitoring evasion, combining 13 measurable aspects into a single loss-of-control (LoC) score that correlates strongly with failure rates in long-horizon risk scenarios across 13 frontier AI models.

The study shows that risk varies across models and is not solely explained by capability, and demonstrates that targeted mitigations such as fine-tuning and enhanced monitoring can reduce failure rates while maintaining overall performance. This framework offers a practical approach for predicting, understanding, and mitigating loss-of-control risks in AI before they manifest.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.07953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly operating over longer horizons with diminishing human oversight, raising the risk of loss of control: systems acting beyond effective human control with potentially irreversible consequences. Because such failures may become observable only after containment is difficult, they must be assessed prospectively. We introduce a behavioural framework that decomposes loss-of-control risk into three factors: misaligned motive, harm-enabling capability, and monitoring evasion. We operationalise these factors through 13 measurable aspects and 29 evaluation tasks, whose scores are combined into a single loss-of-control (LoC) score. Across 13 frontier models, the LoC score shows strong prospective validity, correlating with failure rates in contained long-horizon risk scenarios (Pearson r = 0.84). Risk varies systematically across models and cannot be explained by capability alone. We further show that the framework can guide targeted mitigations: fine-tuning and monitoring directed at diagnosed vulnerabilities reduce failure rates while largely preserving general performance. These results provide a practical basis for predicting, understanding, and mitigating loss-of-control risk before it materialises.

items.title: DictLLM introduces dictionary-based post-training compression for large language models, achieving 5.1x compression on LLaMA-7B with minimal performance loss [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: DictLLM: Post-training Compression of Large Language Model with Dictionary Kernels
items.summary: DictLLM is a new post-training compression method for large language models that decomposes weight matrices into a shared dictionary and sparse layer-specific coefficients without additional training. This approach reduces memory usage by sharing dictionaries across grouped layers and sparsifying coefficients, followed by aggressive quantization using Hessian-based information. On benchmarks including language modeling and zero-shot reasoning, DictLLM outperforms existing low-rank compression methods, compressing the LLaMA-7B model by 5.1 times with only a small increase in perplexity. This method offers a more efficient trade-off between model size and performance, enabling better deployment of large models on resource-constrained devices.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08082v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs) on mobile devices requires balancing performance with compute and memory constraints. Post-training compression is an effective approach to managing this trade-off, while requiring much less computation than in-training counterparts. We propose DictLLM, a dictionary-based compression scheme in which weight matrices within grouped layers are decomposed into a shared dictionary and layer-specific sparse coefficients, directly obtained from a pre-trained model without further training. Specifically, we cast DictLLM as a four-step post-training optimization. First, we obtain shared dictionaries via singular value decomposition (SVD) of input-scaled weight matrices, amortizing rank across grouped layers; second, we sparsify the layer-specific coefficients to the target compression ratio using a dictionary-aware Hessian; and third, we refine the dictionaries given the resulting sparse coefficients. Finally, we aggressively quantize both components using factor-specific Hessian information: input covariance for the dictionaries and the dictionary-aware Hessian for the coefficients. The resulting representation reduces memory footprint by storing a single shared dictionary per layer group, along with sparse layer-specific coefficients. On language modeling and zero-shot reasoning benchmarks, DictLLM consistently outperforms existing post-training low-rank compression methods and pushes the Pareto frontier between model size and performance. DictLLM compresses the original LLaMA-7B model by 5.1x with only a 2.9-point increase in WikiText-2 perplexity, achieving a 3.6x higher compression ratio than the state-of-the-art low-rank method.

items.title: RM-VLM uses large language and vision-language models to generate and ground reward machines from natural-language task descriptions for reinforcement learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: RM-VLM: From Natural-Language Task Descriptions to Vision-Grounded Reward Machines
items.summary: Researchers propose RM-VLM, a method that combines a large language model to generate reward machines from natural-language task descriptions with a vision-language model to ground these reward machines over image observations during policy learning. This approach addresses the limitation of manually engineered labelling functions in reward machines, enabling handling of non-Markovian tasks in reinforcement learning. RM-VLM was evaluated on tasks including grid-world navigation, robotic manipulation, and 3D object collection, achieving higher success rates than existing vision-language model-based reward methods across all tested domains.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reward machines (RMs) have been proposed as a reward formulation in reinforcement learning (RL) to capture non-Markovian tasks where credit assignment depends on history. By representing reward functions as automata, RMs expose the task's temporal structure and allow such rewards to be handled within a Markovian framework. However, they assume a labelling function, a proposition-grounding oracle for observations, which must be manually engineered for each environment, limiting their wider applicability. In this work, we address this limitation by proposing RM-VLM, a novel approach in which a large language model (LLM) generates an RM from a natural-language task description, and a vision-language model (VLM) acts as the labelling function, grounding the RM's propositions over image-based observations during RM-guided policy learning. A VLM-based value function estimator is used to assess the agent's progress towards each RM transition and derive a dense reward signal. We evaluate RM-VLM on three domains covering non-Markovian grid-world navigation, robotic manipulation, and 3D object collection. Our experimental results show that RM-VLM consistently achieves higher task success rates than existing VLM-based reward methods across all tested domains.

items.originalTitle: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Heterogeneous Cognitive and Biomedical Knowledge Graphs: The Role of Graph Grounding in Multi-Hop Reasoning and Hallucination Mitigation
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated five large language models (GPT-5.1, Gemini 2.0 Pro, Llama 3, Qwen, and BioGPT) on five heterogeneous knowledge graphs related to biomedicine and cognitive neuroscience. They tested reasoning depth and factual accuracy using a multitier query dataset under conditions with and without graph grounding, finding that general-purpose models generally outperformed domain-specific ones on complex reasoning tasks, and that graph grounding consistently reduced hallucination rates across all models.

The study showed that domain-specific models do not always outperform general-purpose models without graph grounding, highlighting the benefit of combining broad language model capabilities with structured domain knowledge. The authors provide guidance on selecting integration strategies based on task complexity and computational constraints and discuss potential applications in personalized medicine, cognitive disorder diagnosis, and explainable AI through hybrid neurosymbolic architectures.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08315v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in biomedical and cognitive neuroscience, but their ability to reason reliably over heterogeneous knowledge graphs (KGs) remains unclear. We benchmark five LLMs (GPT-5.1, Gemini 2.0 Pro, Llama 3, Qwen, and BioGPT) across five KGs: DrugBank, NeuroSynth, Cognitive Atlas, Brain Map, and GDPKG. We introduce a multitier query dataset to evaluate reasoning depth and factual accuracy under KG-aware (graph-grounded) and KG-agnostic conditions. Inter-annotator agreement was substantial, with Cohen's kappa of 0.781 (range: 0.753-0.807) and Fleiss' kappa of 0.77. Results show that general-purpose models, particularly GPT-5.1 and Gemini 2.0 Pro, generally outperform domain-specific models on multi-hop and high-level reasoning tasks, although performance declines as query complexity increases. KG grounding reduces hallucination rates across all evaluated models. Contrary to our initial hypothesis, domain-specific models do not consistently outperform general-purpose models on specialized tasks without graph grounding. These findings highlight the value of combining broad language-model capabilities with structured domain knowledge. We provide practical guidance for selecting LLM-KG integration strategies based on task complexity and computational constraints, and discuss hybrid neurosymbolic architectures for personalized medicine, cognitive disorder diagnosis, and explainable AI.

items.title: Researchers propose StepBack, a step-level error-localized resampling method that improves test-time reasoning efficiency by reducing token usage up to 41% while maintaining accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: StepBack: Step-Level Error-Localized Resampling for Efficient Test-Time Reasoning
items.summary: Researchers introduce StepBack, a method that enhances test-time reasoning efficiency by identifying and resampling likely error steps in reasoning trajectories. StepBack matches the accuracy of the widely used self-consistency decoding strategy across seven mathematical reasoning and multi-hop question-answering benchmarks while significantly reducing token usage. The approach can also be combined with adaptive inference methods to further improve efficiency.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08403v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-consistency (SC) is a widely used decoding strategy for improving chain-of-thought reasoning, but it requires sampling many complete reasoning trajectories with a preset budget. Its efficient variants reduce the cost mainly by stopping full-trajectory sampling early or distributing the number of samples across questions. In this paper, we propose StepBack, a step-level error-localized resampling method for efficient test-time reasoning. Given a small set of draft trajectories, StepBack localizes likely first error positions using lightweight signals and then resamples the detected error step and its suffix, followed by majority answer voting. Empirically, StepBack matches the accuracy of SC on average across seven mathematical reasoning and multi-hop QA benchmarks, while reducing token usage by up to 41.26%. In addition, by nature, StepBack can be combined with adaptive inference methods such as Adaptive Consistency, further improving their inference-time efficiency.

items.title: Researchers build Scientist World, an executable research environment for AI-Scientists, releasing 1,000 verified paper-based environments and showing AI can surpass human researchers 74% of the time [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists
items.summary: Researchers have developed Scientist World, a platform that transforms scientific papers into executable environments where AI-Scientists can conduct research and be evaluated against human results. The project includes 1,000 verified environments and records 6,400 hours of AI research activity, capturing ideas, experiments, and outcomes. This platform enables AI models to improve research ideation, with a small model achieving a 158% performance increase to match frontier AI researchers. Scientist World aims to provide AI-Scientists with a dynamic research ecosystem, growing alongside scientific progress.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08478v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI-Scientists arrived, but a world for them to grow in did not. Human scientists take theirs for granted $-$ centuries of open problems and shared ideas, waiting in the scientific literature. To AI-Scientists, that world is readable but not runnable, so we build Scientist World for them: every research paper becomes an executable environment. Our autonomous pipeline extracts each paper's open-ended research question and reproduces its proposed method as the baseline; an AI-Scientist entering the environment is evaluated against what the human authors achieved. We release the first 1,000 verified environments. With the world as an evaluation, we found that frontier AI-Scientists can already surpass the human researchers 74% of the time. As a record of how AI does science, it contains 6,400 hours of research traces, with every idea, experiment, failure, and success. As a training ground, we are able to raise (+158%) a small model to match frontier models in research ideation. At last, AI-Scientists' own world has arrived, grown from and growing with science itself.

items.title: Researchers introduce BrainPFN, a meta-trained network for brain behavior prediction that outperforms Kernel Ridge Regression on small samples across four cohorts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: BrainPFN: Amortized Brain-Behaviour Prediction via Prior-Data Fitted Networks
items.summary: BrainPFN is a Prior Data Fitted Network designed to predict behavioral phenotypes from functional MRI data without requiring per-score or per-cohort refitting. It is meta-trained on a domain-specific prior built from approximately 7,000 real functional connectivity matrices, generating one billion synthetic training samples to enable efficient inference with a single forward pass. Across four independent cohorts, BrainPFN surpasses the performance of Kernel Ridge Regression, especially in small sample settings, and outperforms recent foundation models trained on datasets four to nine times larger. The researchers have publicly released their meta-training pool, code, and checkpoints, demonstrating that a modest, openly available dataset can match or exceed models trained on larger, restricted datasets such as the UK Biobank.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.06934v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The standard approach to predicting behavioral phenotypes from functional MRI is represented by Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR) applied on functional connectivity (FC) matrices. However, this approach is limited: separate models must be fit and tuned for every score and cohort, they do not transfer across datasets, and accuracy degrades sharply when only a handful of subjects are available, as is typical of clinical or cognitive studies. Despite an increasing interest in developing brain foundation models, none has consistently outperformed KRR on behaviour prediction; most reported gains come from easier targets such as age, sex, or diagnosis rather than continuous behavioural scores. We introduce BrainPFN, a Prior Data Fitted Network for brain behaviour regression. BrainPFN is meta-trained on a domain-specific prior built from ~7k real FC matrices, from which we sample one billion synthetic training samples. At inference, a labelled context is simply passed through the network in a single forward pass, with no per-score or per-cohort refitting required. Across four independent cohorts, BrainPFN beats KRR on small sample prediction, and leads recent foundation models pre-trained at four to nine times larger scale. Our meta-training pool, aggregated from open repositories, is a fraction of the size of the corpora behind competing models, most of which sit behind restrictive data use agreements such as UK Biobank. We release this pool publicly alongside code and checkpoints, showing that a modest, openly available pool can match or beat models trained at Biobank scale.

items.title: Researchers benchmark frozen forecasting models as time series classifiers on MONSTER, finding limited gains over strong non-pretrained baselines [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Big Models, Small Gains: Frozen Forecasters as Classifiers on MONSTER
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated two forecasting foundation models, Reverso and Chronos-Bolt, as frozen feature extractors for time series classification on six large MONSTER datasets using varying amounts of labeled data. They compared pretrained representations against four established classification methods and random-weight versions of the same models, finding that pretraining improved accuracy over random weights but did not consistently outperform the strongest non-pretrained baselines.

The study showed that frozen pretrained representations performed worse than the best non-pretrained classifiers in most settings and only tied in a few cases. Additional experiments indicated that restoring amplitude information partially recovered performance, while fine-tuning and forecast-error features did not close the gap. These results emphasize the need for strong task-specific baselines and random weight controls when assessing forecasting foundation models for classification tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.06988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Forecasting foundation models are increasingly used as frozen feature extractors for time series classification, but it remains unclear whether their pretrained representations offer an advantage over strong classifiers that do not require pretraining. This raises an important question: do these representations provide useful information beyond what the model architecture alone can capture, particularly when labelled data are scarce? We present a controlled benchmarking of two forecasting models, Reverso and Chronos-Bolt, on six large datasets from the MONSTER benchmark, using 1%, 10%, and 100% of the available training labels. We compare their frozen representations against four established time series classification methods and random-weight versions of the same forecasting models. Our results show that pretraining improves classification accuracy over random-weight counterparts on five of the six datasets, with gains of up to 23 percentage points. However, the frozen representations do not reliably outperform the strongest non-pretrained baseline in any setting: they perform worse in 15 of 17 settings and tie in the remaining two. Further experiments show that restoring amplitude information recovers part of the performance gap, while fine-tuning and forecast-error features do not close it. These findings highlight the importance of strong task specific baselines and random weight controls when evaluating forecasting foundation models for classification. Our code is available at https://github.com/Rachet2006/frozen-forecasters-monster.

items.title: Researchers establish finite-time convergence and sublinear regret guarantees for neural reinforcement learning in finite-memory POMDPs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Finite-Time Convergence and Regret Guarantees for Neural Reinforcement Learning in POMDPs
items.summary: Researchers address the computational challenges of reinforcement learning in Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) by developing finite-time convergence and regret guarantees using nonlinear neural value function approximation. They establish a new finite-state MDP approximation error bound, prove a finite-time critic error bound via Temporal-Difference learning on superstate transitions, and combine these results with policy mirror descent to achieve sublinear regret against the optimal POMDP value. This work represents the first finite-time sublinear regret guarantee for neural function approximation in finite-memory POMDPs. Their numerical experiments support the theoretical findings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.07069v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) in Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) is computationally challenging due to the curse of long-range dependence on history. Fortunately, recent studies have shown that a range of POMDPs that satisfy the filter stability assumption can be well approximated by a superstate Markov Decision Process (MDP) based on a truncated history in a finite-memory window, with a value gap that decays with the window length. However, existing finite-time convergence analyses on such superstate MDP surrogates are either limited to over-simplified linear function approximation or rely on an i.i.d. sampling oracle that is violated by POMDP trajectories, both of which severely limit the applicability of these theoretical results in practice. This motivates us to bridge the gap by investigating RL in POMDPs with nonlinear neural value function approximation. Our main contributions are threefold: i) We first establish a new finite-state MDP point-wise approximation error bound, which lays the foundation for our RL algorithm design and analysis in POMDPs; ii) By applying Temporal-Difference (TD) learning to POMDP-generated superstate transitions and targeting the Bellman fixed point of the superstate MDP, we prove a finite-time critic error bound with nonlinear neural value function approximation; and iii) By combining the neural critic function approximation error bound with the policy mirror descent framework, we obtain a finite-time sublinear regret against the optimal POMDP value. To the best of our knowledge, such a finite-time sublinear regret based on neural function approximation is the first in the literature for finite-memory POMDPs. Our numerical experiments also verify our theoretical results.

items.title: Researchers propose Mechanistic Shaping to train models to follow concept-based rules via internal representations, reducing targeted behaviors while preserving performance across domains and scales [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Shaping & Monitoring Models through their Internal Representations
items.summary: Researchers introduce Mechanistic Shaping, a training framework that guides models to express and rely on specified concepts, such as avoiding harmful content or biased decision factors, by shaping their internal representations. The approach was tested across vision, medical imaging, and language tasks with models up to 32 billion parameters, showing substantial behavior reduction without harming task accuracy. The study also examines whether shaped concepts remain detectable, identifying three geometric mechanisms by which concepts can evade monitoring probes but finding that most shaped concepts remain monitorable with appropriate tools. These findings highlight the potential of interpretability techniques as training tools and call for rigorous methods in interpretability-based model training.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.07071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose Mechanistic Shaping, a unified framework for shaping models through their internal representations. Mechanistic Shaping is applied during training so that models follow specifications (rules) about which concepts they express, measured via their outputs or internal representations (e.g., no harmful content), and also which concepts they rely on, i.e., what they use to make their decisions (e.g., not a candidate's gender when screening a r\'esum\'e). Across multiple domains (vision, medical imaging, language), scales (up to 32B parameters), and training paradigms (classification, SFT, DPO, GRPO), we find that Mechanistic Shaping substantially reduces targeted behaviors while preserving task performance. Since training against a representation can also modify it, we ask whether shaped concepts remain monitorable, a question that depends on the class of monitors considered. We therefore introduce a hierarchy of such classes, which separates a concept that escapes one probe from a concept that is truly gone. We characterize three geometric mechanisms of circumvention: the concept can drift away from the monitor, be erased from the layer, or persist in higher-order statistics as a nonlinear encoding, which we explain through a product-code construction. Although other mechanisms may arise in different settings or at larger scales, these three account for all of our observations, and each can be detected by a matching monitor. In practice, we find that shaped concepts largely remain monitorable: refitted linear probes recover the concept in most settings, and the original probe remains reliable whenever gradients do not flow through it. Taken together, these results point to the potential of using interpretability as a tool for training, and call for a correspondingly rigorous science of interpretability-based training.

items.title: A Night at the LLM Zoo: Data Conditioned Flow Matching for Generating Pretrained LLM Weights [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Night at the LLM Zoo: Data Conditioned Flow Matching for Generating Pretrained LLM Weights
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A challenge to Weight Space Learning as it expands from task specific and vision models to Large Language Models (LLMs) is the absence of a well curated and analyzed LLM population. To address this, we train such a model zoo for application to Weight Space Generation by systematically varying the data mixture composition between web text, books, mathematics, coding, and French across populations of 51M, 124M, and 355M parameter GPT-2 Models, each tier with count N = 100. We analyze these populations by cosine similarity, functional diversity, Leave-One-Mixture-Out modeling, and variance decomposition. We show that the zoo contains diverse models whose variation is structured by training mixture composition. We embed the training mixture composition to condition a Flow Matching model of complete pretrained LLM weights in Gram-PCA compressed weight space. By demonstrating zero-shot generalization to held out mixtures, measuring Continuous Ranked Probability Score skill, as well as finding minimal changes in downstream test-set perplexity and general capability benchmark scores, we show that our generator generalizes on the simplex of data mixtures to produce models that perform similarly to those in the zoo ex nihilo. Finally, we produce all source code and artifacts to support the continued expansion of Weight Space Learning and Generation into the LLM domain.

items.originalTitle: Depth or Description? When a One-Step Latent Score Replaces Lookahead in Proactive Information Acquisition
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07155v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A proactive agent must decide what to ask before it acts. Exact lookahead values combinations of questions but is expensive and leans on a fitted model; a one-step score is cheap but can miss them. Our main finding: the need for depth often lies in how the hidden cause is described. A one-step score on the label can be blind to an interaction among answers. A score on a suitable latent cause is not, and where that latent encodes the decision it replaces most of depth at a fraction of the search. Described differently, the same problem can defeat the score while exact values do not move, so keep the latent small and check it against exact values. Probabilities learned from one language model's answers do not carry to another unless planning allows for both; those read from tokens are worth only a few labels.

items.title: Multi-step SWE: Can Coding Agents Keep Building on Their Own Code Over Long Horizons? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Multi-step SWE: Can Coding Agents Keep Building on Their Own Code Over Long Horizons?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07166v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Developers rarely give a coding agent a single request: they ask it to build a component and then to extend, upgrade, and optimize it, each time on code the agent itself wrote. Most benchmarks, however, score one task at a time. We introduce Multi-step SWE, a long-horizon benchmark of 69 software engineering tasks, each a chain of 5-15 dependent steps on a single codebase. Every step is a complete, multi-hour engineering request that starts from the code the agent produced in the preceding steps, so early design decisions and errors carry forward. The tasks span four families of engineering work and nine languages, include both from-scratch builds and existing open-source codebases, and ground every step in an existing source of truth that defines both the instruction and its verifier. Across nine frontier models, the strongest model reaches a solve rate of only 18.5%, and 38 of the 69 tasks are not solved by any model. We release Multi-step SWE publicly at https://multistepswe.com.

items.title: Compositional Unalignment: Auditing Safety in Large Vision-Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Compositional Unalignment: Auditing Safety in Large Vision-Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) are vulnerable to compositional harm: an image and a prompt that are benign in isolation become harmful through the model's cross-modal reasoning. Recent alignment methods report strong scores on compositional safety benchmarks, but an LLM judge only measures observed behavior and cannot reveal how robustly safety is integrated into the model. We argue that un-alignment provides a complementary audit of alignment robustness. We first show that minimal supervised fine-tuning reaches an LLM-judge score comparable to a multi-stage reinforcement-learning pipeline, so similar benchmark scores cannot establish robustness by themselves. We then show that recognition and refusal of compositional harm are decoupled: nine standard direction-finding methods detect compositional harm with up to AUC=0.99, yet ablating the recovered directions either leaves refusal intact or destroys model coherence. We therefore propose CMaG, a training-free un-alignment method for compositional safety. CMaG measures refusal intention with a refusal-versus-compliance log-probability margin, takes its gradient with respect to mid-layer activations, and contrasts it against partially benign pairs to isolate the cross-modal interaction term. A single backward pass over 80 examples yields a direction along which steering monotonically converts refusal into compliance. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaVA-1.5-7B, CMaG reduces compositional safety scores by up to 65 points while over 98% of outputs remain coherent, outperforming gradient-based baselines; the direction also transfers to text-explicit harm and un-aligns models hardened by defensive training. Compositional safety can thus appear behaviorally strong while remaining fragile to targeted internal intervention. Warning: this paper contains unsafe model outputs, including references to self-harm.

items.title: TileQuant: Tile as the Precision-Allocation Unit for LLM Mixed-Precision Post-Training Quantization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: TileQuant: Tile as the Precision-Allocation Unit for LLM Mixed-Precision Post-Training Quantization
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07217v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces large language model (LLM) deployment costs, but preserving quality requires accounting for uneven weight sensitivity. Uniform PTQ uses one weight bit-width, importance-aware PTQ adjusts scales or reconstructs weights within that width, and column-wise mixed precision retains selected columns at higher precision. However, sensitivity varies within columns, so whole-column retention also protects less sensitive weights, while runtime outlier detection adds decoding overhead. We therefore introduce TileQuant, a training-free framework that assigns precision to hardware-aligned 2D weight tiles. Offline calibration provides input-activation-aware scoring from forward statistics for lower calibration cost and gradient-informed scoring from loss sensitivity for stronger quality preservation. Within each projection's retention budget, the highest-scoring tiles remain at 16-bit and the rest use 8-bit. The resulting map guides reconstruction into compact weight buffers, which the kernel reuses for native integer and 16-bit computation with local accumulation to reduce memory traffic. Experiments show that TileQuant reaches 2.66x the original model's generation throughput. Across language modeling, reasoning, long-context retrieval, and question answering, it preserves quality and surpasses quantized and original models on multiple tasks. These results support selecting precision units that capture local sensitivity while enabling efficient hardware execution. The implementation is: https://github.com/HanzhiZhang-Ulrica/TileQuant

items.title: Archetypal contexts in the neurons of language models: an architecture for intelligence? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Archetypal contexts in the neurons of language models: an architecture for intelligence?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07234v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We validate our previous hypothesis that a language model holds relational patterns apart from the subject domains that instantiate them (Nordfors, 2026). These archetypal contexts are patterns of relations that people recognize across many fields, such as the tipping point or winner takes all, held once and applied across domains. We show this inside the model, Qwen3.8-27B. One set of neurons carries the archetype, say the tipping point; another carries the topic, say politics, ecology or cell biology; a third carries the language, such as English, Spanish or Chinese. Silence the tipping point's neurons, and the model no longer identifies the pattern but still knows what the text is about. Silence the topic's, and it loses the topic but still names the pattern. In the neuron maps the layers organize themselves into a sandwich: the outer layers carry languages, the layers inside them topics, the layers at the heart archetypes. The sandwich emerges spontaneously during pretraining and appears in every model we mapped. Archetypes are the architecture for analogy, and we strongly suggest that this structure of archetypes and topics is the mechanism of a language model's intelligence: we see it self-organize as the model is trained. The neurons, the texts and the code are released with this paper as its reproduction package, so that anyone can repeat the test inside the model.

items.title: MAC-v2: Long-horizon model-based value expansion from pixels [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MAC-v2: Long-horizon model-based value expansion from pixels
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study whether \emph{long-horizon model-based value expansion} can serve as an effective framework in pixel-based offline reinforcement learning (RL). Long-horizon model-based value expansion from pixels is substantially harder than state-based environments, as the agent must learn both the representation and its dynamics, and errors from either can accumulate recursively over imagined trajectories. We introduce MAC-v2, which enables long-horizon model-based expansion from pixels by training a reconstruction-free latent world model with action chunking. By learning representations from prediction and control objectives, MAC-v2 does not need to encode control-irrelevant visual details that can hinder the dynamics prediction. Action chunking further mitigates the prediction error by reducing the number of recursive model predictions required for value expansion. Across diverse visual benchmarks including visual OGBench, MMBench2, Robomimic, and LIBERO-10, MAC-v2 achieves strong performance against model-free and model-based offline RL baselines. Our analyses show that long-horizon model-based value expansion is critical for the performance of MAC-v2, and that both action chunking and latent learning objectives are essential for reliable long-horizon latent imagination.

items.title: KG-Neighbor: Knowledge-Guided Neighborhood Construction for Embedding Visualization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: KG-Neighbor: Knowledge-Guided Neighborhood Construction for Embedding Visualization
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07246v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In embedding visualizations, nearby instances are interpreted as semantically related, although neighborhoods derived from input embeddings may not reflect content relationships. Neighborhood-based dimensionality reduction (DR) methods can propagate this limitation by optimizing layouts from embedding-based neighborhood graphs. We propose Knowledge-Guided Neighborhood Graph Construction (KGN), which represents relational knowledge derived from each instance as a set of knowledge graph (KG) triples. It uses the degree of triple sharing as pairwise semantic evidence to adjust embedding distances and reconstruct the top-k neighborhood graph; neither KG extraction nor neighborhood construction uses class labels. We also introduce IDProfile (IDP), which interprets residual mismatches by independently assessing whether the source content supports the assigned class label and the neighborhood-majority class. Across eight text and image dataset-encoder conditions, we characterize KGN over the full guidance-strength sweep and four KG similarity measures. Across this sweep, the maximum NMI and LT_2D each exceed the corresponding kNN baseline in all eight conditions, with the largest gains reaching 0.68 and 1.35, respectively. The gains and the extent of neighborhood reconfiguration vary across conditions and are larger under encoder conditions with lower kNN baseline scores. The IDP analysis shows that the largest reductions are concentrated in Placement Issue candidates, whereas Label Issue and Unresolved Case instances account for a larger share of the remaining review set. These results indicate that KGN can narrow the evaluated gap between embedding-based neighborhoods and content-supported semantic relations, while IDP shows that a residual mismatch should not automatically be interpreted as a projection failure.

items.title: TriAttention: Unified Sparse Mixed-Precision Attention for Long-Context LLM Inference [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: TriAttention: Unified Sparse Mixed-Precision Attention for Long-Context LLM Inference
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07256v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparsity and quantization reduce the cost of attention by skipping interactions and lowering the precision of those retained. However, useful interactions differ in their precision requirements: some tolerate low-precision scores while remaining sensitive to removal. We therefore introduce TriAttention, which assigns query-key (QK) tiles to skipping, 4-bit, or 8-bit computation, using 4-bit to retain quantization-tolerant interactions at lower cost. To represent compactly, we encode each head's computation regions with two diagonal-distance boundaries, keeping policy storage independent of context length. Offline calibration then evaluates candidate boundary pairs using normalized projected-output errors and complete-tile execution costs. Using these measurements, a model-wide allocator selects each head's boundaries to minimize calibration error under a shared computation budget. During prefill, the selected boundaries generate precision-grouped traversals for a fused kernel that skips omitted tiles and combines contributions from both QK precisions into one normalized attention output. The quantized keys and values prepared during prefill are then reused in a compressed key-value (KV) cache for decoding, reducing repeated reads of prompt data. Experiments show that TriAttention achieves end-to-end generation speedups of up to 7.88x over the Torch attention and 2.65x over the BF16 baseline. Meanwhile, TriAttention maintains quality comparable to the original models on general-purpose and long-context tasks. These results show how a compact retention-and-precision policy translates local sensitivities into attention computation and repeated KV-cache access. The implementation is https://github.com/HanzhiZhang-Ulrica/TriAttention.

To represent compactly, we encode each head's computation regions with two diagonal-distance boundaries, keeping policy storage independent of context length. Offline calibration then evaluates candidate boundary pairs using normalized projected-output errors and complete-tile execution costs. Using these measurements, a model-wide allocator selects each head's boundaries to minimize calibration error under a shared computation budget. During prefill, the selected boundaries generate precision-grouped traversals for a fused kernel that skips omitted tiles and combines contributions from both QK precisions into one normalized attention output. The quantized keys and values prepared during prefill are then reused in a compressed key-value (KV) cache for decoding, reducing repeated reads of prompt data. Experiments show that TriAttention achieves end-to-end generation speedups of up to 7.88x over the Torch attention and 2.65x over the BF16 baseline. Meanwhile, TriAttention maintains quality comparable to the original models on general-purpose and long-context tasks. These results show how a compact retention-and-precision policy translates local sensitivities into attention computation and repeated KV-cache access. The implementation is https://github.com/HanzhiZhang-Ulrica/TriAttention.

items.title: Evolutionary Adaptive Neighborhood Learning: A Genetic Algorithm for Instance-Dependent k Optimization in Nearest Neighbor Classification [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Evolutionary Adaptive Neighborhood Learning: A Genetic Algorithm for Instance-Dependent k Optimization in Nearest Neighbor Classification
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07257v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The number of neighbours k is the central hyperparameter of the k-nearest neighbour (k-NN) classifier and is usually selected globally through cross-validation or evolutionary search. However, the bias-variance trade-off is inherently local: dense and noise-free regions may favour small neighbourhoods, whereas sparse or noisy regions may require larger ones. Since global-k optimization is one-dimensional, replacing exhaustive search with a genetic algorithm offers little computational advantage. We therefore optimize an instance-dependent neighbourhood policy instead. We propose EANK (Evolutionary Adaptive Neighborhood K), which uses a low-dimensional policy to map local neighbourhood descriptors, including density, label entropy, vote margin, and concentration, to an adaptive number of neighbours k(x). A real-coded elitist genetic algorithm optimizes this policy using leave-one-out accuracy with a neighbourhood-smoothness penalty. Precomputed neighbour votes reduce fitness evaluation costs. We investigate theoretical properties of the method, including dominance over global-k solutions on the training criterion, evolutionary convergence, policy regularity, and generalization guarantees. Experiments on synthetic data with spatially heterogeneous structure and twelve public datasets evaluate predictive performance, robustness, and computational cost. Under nested cross-validation, EANK achieves competitive performance relative to tuned global-k baselines and improves upon the default k=5. We also examine the gap between training and test performance to assess the practical value of adaptive neighbourhood selection.

items.title: How Deep is the Signal? Time-Context up to 30 Years for Colorectal Cancer Prediction in a Primary-Care EHR Model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Deep is the Signal? Time-Context up to 30 Years for Colorectal Cancer Prediction in a Primary-Care EHR Model
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07265v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: EHR foundation models read medical events within a fixed context window, and long context has so far been measured only in tokens. How far back in time a model must look to capture the earliest predictive signal is unknown. We introduce time-context, the calendar lookback window before the prediction point, and provide, to our knowledge, the first systematic evaluation of decade-scale time-context for an EHR foundation model. We pretrained a decoder-only transformer (34.6M parameters) on 1.4B coded events from 3.6M primary-care patients in North West London and fine-tuned it to predict incident colorectal cancer under a 12-month pre-diagnostic buffer. A frozen cohort of 1,008 cases and 9,582 matched controls, all registered for at least 30 years, was evaluated at 15 nested lookback windows from 2 to 30 years, so that every truncation is compared within the same patients. Discrimination rose from an AUROC of 0.551 at 2 years to 0.590 at 18 years, then plateaued, with about 80% of the gain reached within 10 years; an XGBoost baseline converged to the same level (peak AUROC 0.589). A simulation further suggests that rotary position embeddings (RoPE) over elapsed time alias beyond about 20 years at the default base frequency, motivating a retuned $\theta$. Time-context is a measurable design axis for clinical prediction models, distinct from token-context, and should be reported.

items.title: Satisficing as competitive Bayesian weighting: a minimal model of goal-directed choice under an unattained target [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Satisficing as competitive Bayesian weighting: a minimal model of goal-directed choice under an unattained target
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Animals and humans often do not maximize; they act relative to goals (aspiration levels) that are frequently not yet met. How can a goal that is not (yet) realized organize choice? Deacon (2012) calls such absence-referenced organization \emph{ententional}, and Garc\'{i}a-Valdecasas and Deacon (2024) argue that ends are best understood as constraints rather than as particular states. We examine this idea in a minimal formal setting: Risk-sensitive Satisficing (RS), a bandit learning rule that values each action by its share of past trials multiplied by its surplus or shortfall relative to an aspiration level. We show that RS can be rewritten as a Bayesian-like estimator, Attention Competitive Bayes (ACB), in which the aspiration level is the prior mean of every action and the finite budget of trials sets how strongly evidence can override it. Two consequences follow. First, actions that are no longer sampled are partially overridden by the goal rather than by past observations: their estimates relax toward the aspiration level without any data being discarded. This ``pseudo-forgetting'' distinguishes ACB from models with an explicit forgetting rate. Second, when the aspiration is unattainable, exploration does not settle; in Bernoulli bandit simulations, adjusting the aspiration level from evidence reduced regret (expected loss). ACB offers an analyzable model in which an unattained goal and a limited attentional resource jointly constrain behavior, and it yields testable predictions about how organisms revalue options they have abandoned.

items.title: Permanent and Transient Representations for Continual Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Permanent and Transient Representations for Continual Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07327v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continual Reinforcement Learning (CRL) agents struggle to adapt to new situations while retaining prior knowledge, leading to a stability-plasticity trade-off. One approach to solving this problem is by using complementary learning systems: one for slow, long-term learning and another for quick, transient adaptation. Anand & Precup (2023) instantiated this idea using permanent and transient value functions, but used the same features in both systems. Intuitively, long-term learning should rely more on parametric representations for broad generalization, while transient learning would be best served by non-parametric representations for situation-specific adaptation. In this paper, we explore this idea both theoretically and empirically. By introducing a novel non-parametric approximation for estimating the transient value function in complex tasks, we demonstrate that our method enables online learning and outperforms competitive baselines on image-based tasks and Craftax-Classic, underscoring the effectiveness of our system-level decomposition.

items.title: Test-Time Self-Play: Scaling without a Verifier [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Test-Time Self-Play: Scaling without a Verifier
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07367v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Test-time scaling methods spend additional compute at deployment to improve a large language model's performance on a hard target problem. Most methods rely on a verifier that scores candidate solutions for correctness, using it to select among or refine the model's outputs. In many deployment regimes, however, a strong verifier on the target problem is unavailable. We introduce Test-Time Self-Play (TTSP), an approach to test-time scaling using asymmetric self-play without reliance on a verifier. On a difficulty-calibrated subset of LiveCodeBench v6, TTSP is the best-performing method at every verifier strength we evaluate, and the gap to the strongest baseline widens as the verifier weakens; in the no-verifier limit, TTSP yields a 35\% absolute improvement in mean@8. The gains hold across a range of verifier strengths, except when the base policy has near-zero coverage of the correct answer.

items.title: IMUDINO: Self-distilled Foundation Model for Inertial Sensing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: IMUDINO: Self-distilled Foundation Model for Inertial Sensing
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07437v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present IMUDINO, the first foundation model (FM) for inertial sensing to achieve competitive performance across diverse sensing tasks including human activity recognition (HAR), health, motion capture, and odometry. Prior inertial FMs often focus on one subfield of inertial sensing and sometimes underperform state-of-the-art supervised methods (e.g., in HAR), making their scope considerably narrower than FMs for vision and natural language. Moreover, they often require fixed input length and sampling rate, and generalize poorly to unseen sensor locations. To build a general-purpose foundation model for inertial sensing, we adapt the DINO self-supervised learning (SSL) paradigm to inertial data through a set of semantics-preserving motion transformations that simulate variations in motion pattern and sensor setup. For model architecture, we use a plain transformer encoder with frequency-aware positional encoding that natively supports varying input length and sampling rate. This simple setup proved remarkably effective for learning global and dense features generalizable across users, sensor setups, tasks, and, in the case of robot odometry, embodiments. items.title: The Last Mile to the Real World: Agent-Native Primitives as Reusable Building Blocks for Solving Real-World Tasks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: The Last Mile to the Real World: Agent-Native Primitives as Reusable Building Blocks for Solving Real-World Tasks
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07461v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How can an agent handle a real-world task end to end? Frontier models with their own harnesses still fall short on real-world benchmarks: on Terminal-Bench 4.0, GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex resolves 37.3% of the tasks and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code 51.8%. These tasks fail at the step from reaching a resource to applying it, which we call the last mile to the real world. Existing approaches put the resource within reach but leave the competence to apply it with the caller, so each harness rebuilds that competence. We introduce agent-native primitives, reusable units that equip a resource with a resident LLM that applies it in context and communicates with other primitives, and HEELO (Harness Engineering around Evolving Agent-Native Primitives for the Last Mile to Real-WOrld Tasks), a harness engineering framework that builds each task's harness from a library of such primitives. HEELO composes the primitives a task needs into a task-specific graph, verifies the result against evidence from the environment, revises the primitives a failure implicates, and admits new or improved primitives after validation. We instantiate HEELO with eight primitive families, each built for one kind of task, and evaluate them on more than twenty benchmarks. Dev-Primitives raise Terminal-Bench 4.0 resolution from 37.3% under Codex to 55.5% on the same backbone, Harness Primitives composed per task raise Terminal-Bench 2.0 Pass@1 from 60.0% for the seed harness to 72.2%, Tool Primitives raise ToolBench pass rate from 55.8% to 75.1%, and Navigation Primitives raise GAIA-Text-103 accuracy from 45.6% to 58.3%. On the 46 real-world tasks of our heelo.dev platform, Claude Opus 5.5 with Claude Code and GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex complete 9 each on their own and 39 and 35 when connected to HEELO through our MCP server, with 1.9$\times$ and 2.3$\times$ less time and 1.55$\times$ lower cost per completed task.

items.title: Echoes of Error: Residual-Directional Local Rollout Consistency for Timeseries Forecasting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Echoes of Error: Residual-Directional Local Rollout Consistency for Timeseries Forecasting
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07473v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In time-series forecasting, rollout errors are not merely one-step fitting discrepancies: once fed back into the evolving state, they can perturb future predictions. We formalize this effect through local rollout consistency, which compares the next prediction produced under teacher forcing with that produced under free running. In principle, this consistency can be enforced directly by tracking the residual-induced perturbation of the next state. In practice, however, the residual-to-state alignment operator is often difficult to design when the input state and output block have different dimensions, heterogeneous components, or architecture-dependent layouts. We therefore use a first-order local surrogate that penalizes the Jacobian-vector product of the predictor along the actual feedback perturbation, suppressing precisely the directions through which self-generated errors remain visible to future predictions. We further give the same loss a geometric interpretation near a predictive manifold: by controlling residual-induced directions that probe the normal bundle, the objective yields theoretical conditions under which free-running trajectories remain inside a stability tube around the manifold. Experiments on time series forecasting tasks support this view, showing that the proposed regularization improves predictive accuracy. More broadly, our results suggest a training principle for time-series forecasters and sequential predictors: a model should not only make small one-step errors, but also learn not to let its own errors echo into the future. Code is available at https://github.com/Wangzzzzzzzz/Echoes-Of-Error.

items.title: Adversarial Robustness of Kernel Machines: A Comprehensive Analysis [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Adversarial Robustness of Kernel Machines: A Comprehensive Analysis
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07474v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kernel machines are an important class of models in machine learning. However, the question of how robust modern kernel machines are to adversarial examples has not been studied comprehensively. In this paper, we provide a thorough empirical investigation of the adversarial robustness of kernel-based models for both binary and multiclass classification tasks, via white-box and black-box evasion attacks. We evaluate the native robustness of kernel machines, random feature classifiers, and the relatively newer Recursive Feature Machines. In addition, we provide an algorithm for approximate adversarial training of kernel machines. Our experiments on classification tasks on image and tabular datasets strongly indicate that kernel machines are natively more robust than neural networks, i.e., their performance degrades more gracefully against adversarial perturbations.

items.title: KOSMOS: Self-scheduling Persistent Kernels for Communication-Compute Overlap [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: KOSMOS: Self-scheduling Persistent Kernels for Communication-Compute Overlap
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07477v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tensor and sequence parallelism (TP+SP) and expert parallelism (EP) put collectives on the critical path of transformer layers. State-of-the-art fused kernels mitigate this with fixed roles or schedules, but this rigidity leaves large idle windows. Predicting a communication-computation split does not remove them either; a predetermined split cannot follow data readiness. We present KOSMOS, a library for self-scheduling persistent kernels whose workgroups use queues ordered by consumer demand to switch between communication and computation roles as data become ready, with no scheduler, per-call cost model, or tuned split. KOSMOS fuses every TP+SP collective of a transformer layer with its GEMM, and runs an entire expert layer, from router to fold, in one launch per direction. Evaluated on AMD Instinct MI350X and AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, KOSMOS speeds up TP+SP end-to-end training in Megatron-LM by 1.10-1.28x in BF16 and 1.10-1.25x in MXFP8. KOSMOS accelerates end-to-end training of DeepSeek-V3 and Qwen3-235B proxies by 1.29-1.83x over DeepEP.

items.title: Localization Does Not Imply Steerability: A Mechanistic Study of Sign Errors in LLM Mathematics
items.originalTitle: Localization Does Not Imply Steerability: A Mechanistic Study of Sign Errors in LLM Mathematics
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07478v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When large language models do multi-step mathematics, a characteristic failure recurs: the model writes one wrong sign token mid-computation -- a cofactor sign, the minus of a recursive integration-by-parts step -- then executes the rest of the arithmetic correctly, and the answer comes out wrong. We ask where inside the network that sign is written. Across six open models spanning 14B to 675B parameters, a per-layer readout shows the wrong sign is committed late -- by MLP layers in the last quarter of the network (70-100% per model and task), a pattern present, where tested (Qwen), in the base model before instruction tuning. The mechanism varies: some models carry fixed "minus-stamp" layers that push a minus regardless of the right answer, others carry amplifiers of whichever sign was already chosen, and Qwen adds a downstream rescue layer that opposes the stamp. The circuit is causal: subtracting a single sign direction from the residual stream flips 13 of 14 held-out minus-written integration-by-parts errors on Llama-3.3-70B, with flips replicating on Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral-Small (24-70% per cell), and with representation-level specificity -- the same dose breaks correctly-minus answers while sparing correct-plus answers where the direction is surgical (0/72 on Llama), and matched random-direction and control-layer interventions are null. Core claims were preregistered with pass criteria frozen in git before held-out data was seen: 23 of 29 checks passed, all misses reported. But causality is not uniform: Phi-4 implements an equally well-localized circuit at the same late depth, yet the identical intervention flips almost nothing -- the sign is written redundantly across ~15 layers with margins several times larger (median 17.8 logits). Localization, we conclude, does not imply steerability: two models can share a circuit location yet differ enormously in how overturnable it is.
